dossier.public_summary: The 0.54-day dip is on the target star, but it sits exactly on the star's own spot period and its depth doubles and halves between sectors while the star varies by thousands of ppm. The transit shape and much-too-long duration require the star to be far less dense than measured, so the signal is the star's pulsating variability rather than a planet.

reasons.why: Dip period is identical to the star's spot period in all 4 sectors (false alarm down to 1e-181). Coherent phase-curve amplitude 5054 ppm (ratio_to_depth=1.259, chi2=724.6/9, variability_chi2_dof=80.51) shows this is pulsation/variability leaking into the box, not a separate body.

Depth is not stationary even within the same pipeline (SPOC p_constant=4.20652301049839e-07). Sector depths scale with variability amplitude (1893 ppm in low-amplitude sector 33, 3924 ppm in high-amplitude sector 6, 6420 ppm in sector 87); not expected for a true transit.
reasons.value: p_constant=2.458e-13, depth_change_pct=108.9, SPOC 2-min depths 3924 vs 1893 ppm, QLP depths 6420 ppm

reasons.why: Observed duration 0.9812 h is much longer than the 0.5958 h central duration for the TIC star, and the transit shape requires an implausibly low stellar density, indicating the 'transit' is a variability feature stretched by spot evolution rather than a planet occulter.

On-target centroid rules out a neighbour eclipse, and odd/even diff_sigma=0.278 and no secondary support a single dip morphology, but they cannot distinguish a flat-bottomed spot harmonic from a planet. A V-shape (v_sigma=-2.724) and 1.65x duration are both better explained as variability than a grazing planet when combined with the rotation and depth-change evidence.
